.. 1 .. Anticipatory Bail No.797/2015 (Order below Exhibit 1) Order below Exhibit 1 in Anticipatory Bail Appln. No. 797/2015 This application is filed by applicant namely Abdullah Abdul Ghani Shaikh for his release on bail under section 438 of Cr.P.C. in connection with C.R.No.I-323/2015 registered at Mumbra police station on the basis of the complaint for offence punishable under section 354 of I.P.C. and section 8 of Protection of Children From Sexual Offences Act (hereinafter in short referred to as P.O.C.S.O. Act) It was contended and argued that the applicant have been falsely involved in this crime with the allegation of outraging modesty of the minor daughter of the complainant. It is further contended and argued that applicant has never indulged in any such activity as alleged. It is further contended and argued that the applicant had filed complaint against anti-social element in their locality and had refused to give them money and therefore he is falsely involved in this crime. It is further contended and argued that same complaint had previously filed complaint against the applicant making same allegations in connection same girl and in that crime the applicant was granted anticipatory bail and now just to see that he is sent behind bars, this complaint with same allegations is filed. It is also submitted that looking to the nature of allegation the custodial interrogation of the applicant is not required. It is further submitted that the applicant is permanent resident of the address given and that if the present applicant/accused is released on bail, he will co-operate with the investigation and therefore the applicant is entitled to be released on anticipatory bail. 2] The application is objected to on behalf of prosecution by filing reply and it was contended and argued that at the time of incident the victim girl had gone to the shop of applicant for purchasing stationery articles and at that time the applicant outraged her modesty by moving hand over her chest and below waist and by blinking eye at her. It is further contended and argued that the accused had committed such act in past with same girl and now has repeated the offence. It is further .. 2 .. Anticipatory Bail No.797/2015 (Order below Exhibit 1) contended and argued that the applicant had threated the son of the complainant to take back the complaint previously lodged making same allegations. It is further submitted that in such circumstance in order to make thorough investigation, the custodial interrogation of the applicant is necessary. It is further submitted that if the applicant is released on anticipatory bail, there is possibility of the applicant threatening the complainant and victim girl which may hamper the investigation and even the applicant may abscond and may not be available for trial and may tamper with prosecution evidence. It was therefore contended that the applicant is not entitled to be released on anticipatory bail. 3] As is clear the offences under section 354 of I.P.C. and section 8 of P.O.C.S.O. Act charged against the accused are of serious nature and it is contended that the applicant is arraigned in this crime with the allegation that he had molested a 10 years' old girl namely Zeb by blinking eye at her. However, it is contended by the applicant that he is falsely implicated in the crime on account of previous enmity because he had filed complaint against anti-social elements working in their locality who demanded money from them but he refused. The fact that he had filed such complaint is also clear from the documents produced on record alongwith the application. It is also to be mentioned that even earlier same applicant filed anticipatory bail application no.1180/2014 in which he was granted anticipatory bail in regard to crime registered on the basis of same complainant with same allegations and it is contended that since the applicant is released on bail in that case, another complaint is filed only with a view to harass the applicant. That fact is also clear from the copy of the order passed on 16.06.2014 produced on record and it appears that the applicant is ordered to be released on bail in similar crime registered on the basis of complaint filed by the complainant in regard to same girl. No doubt, on that basis it is argued on behalf of prosecution that the applicant is repeating same .. 3 .. Anticipatory Bail No.797/2015 (Order below Exhibit 1) offence and therefore it would not be desirable to release him on bail in this crime. However, it is to be mentioned that previous enmity between the parties is clear and the fact is also clear that it was the present applicant who had filed complaint earlier and therefore there was enmity between the applicant and complainant and in such circumstance the submission that repeated complaints are filed by the complainant with some motive, appear to be worth consideration. In such circumstance looking to the nature of allegations levelled against the applicant, I am of the view that the custodial interrogation of the applicant is not necessary. 4] Then, it is well settled that at this stage of deciding bail application the evidence on record need not be gone into detail and the main criteria to be considered is whether release of the applicants would hamper the process of investigation or whether the applicants would abscond if released on bail and in case of anticipatory bail whether the custodial interrogation of the applicant is necessary. In that regard, as discussed above, looking to the nature of allegation the custodial interrogation of the applicant do not appear to be necessary. 5] Then, it is contended by the applicant that he is permanent resident of the address given and he will not abscond and he is ready to abide by any conditions imposed. 6] Even the apprehension expressed by the prosecution that the applicant may not be available for investigation or release of applicant on anticipatory bail would hamper the investigation etc., can be taken care of by saddling certain conditions including condition to give attendance to police station and for that purpose there appear no necessity of the custody of the applicant. 7] Then, police also have not reported that during the pendency of this application the applicants have indulged in any unlawful activity in connection the present offence or has not co-operated in investigation. .. 4 .. Anticipatory Bail No.797/2015 (Order below Exhibit 1) 8] In all such circumstance I am of the view that this is a fit case wherein the interim anticipatory bail already granted to the applicant can be confirmed. I therefore pass the following order - ORDER The application is allowed. 2) The interim anticipatory bail granted to the applicant namely Abdullah Abdul Ghani Shaikh vide order 01.04.2015 passed below Exhibit 3 is hereby confirmed. 3) In the event of arrest of the applicant for offence punishable under section 354 of I.P.C. and section 8 of P.O.C.S.O. Act registered under C.R.No.I-323/2015 at Mumbra Police Station, he shall be released on furnishing P.R. bond of Rs.15,000/- [rupees fifteen thousand only] with one surety in the like amount, subject to following conditions - a) The applicant shall attend the concerned police station as and when required till filing of the charge sheet and shall co- operate with the investigating machinery. b) He shall not, directly or indirectly, make any inducement, threat or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the Court or to any police officer. c) He shall not leave India without the previous permission of the Court. d) He shall not tamper with prosecution evidence. Date : 13.07.2015. (Ms.V.V.Virkar) Additional Session Judge-1, Thane.

Judgment CNR No. MHTH01­002238 ­2016 JUDGMENT ( Delivered on this 23rd day of October, 2018 ) 1. The accused is charged for the offences punishable under sections 363, 354, 354(A)(B)(D) r/w. 34 of Indian Penal Code and Sec. 8,12 of Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. Brief facts of the prosecution case are as under :­ 2. On 10.08.2015, at about 4.00 p.m., accused made phone call to the victim and called her on ground floor at about 7.30 p.m. for showing some beneficial facts. Accordingly, victim went on the ground floor and met with the accused. Accused had taken her to Upvan by rickshaw. At that time, friend of the accused was also present with them. She was taken to an isolated place and accused had kissed her and removed her top and moved his hand on her chest and took her close and pressed. His friend caught hold hand of victim. Victim started weeping. Then, accused reached her to her house. After that accused used to give missed call to victim. Mother of victim went to Narishakti Brigade Mahila Sanstha for help and thereafter, went to police station. Mother of victim lodged report at police station. Police had registered offence punishable u/sec. 363, 354, 354(A)(B)(D) r/w. 34 of Indian Penal Code and Sec. 8,12 of Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. After due investigation charge­sheet came to be filed in the court of Sessions. 3 Spl. Case(POCSO) No. 83/2016... Judgment CNR No. MHTH01­002238 ­2016 3. My Ld. Predecessor had framed charge (Exh.2) against the accused for the offences punishable under sections 363, 354, 354(A)(B)(D) r/w. 34 of Indian Penal Code and Sec. 8,12 of Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. Contents of charge were read over and explained to the accused in vernacular language, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. 4. I have recorded statement of accused under section 313 (1)(b) of the Criminal Procedure Code at Exh. 16. Defence of accused is of total denial. Accused has not shown his willingness to examine himself on oath or any other defence witness on his behalf. 5. I have heard APP Shri. Kulkarni for the State and Ld. Advocate Shri. Karle for the accused. 6. On perusal of record and evidence on record, following points arise from my determination and consideration and I have recorded my findings thereon for the reasons as stated below:­ POINTS FINDINGS 1. Does the prosecution prove that the In the negative. accused along with absconding accused Sameer on 10.08.2015 at about 7.30 p.m. at Stedium Tube, Mahatma Phule Road, Near Mahagiri, Thane and Upvan, Thane, in furtherance of their common intention, kidnapped victim from the lawful guardianship of her parents and thereby committed an offence punishable under Sec. 363 r/w.34 of IPC? 4 Spl. Case(POCSO) No. 83/2016... Judgment CNR No. MHTH01­002238 ­2016 2. Does the prosecution prove that the In the negative. accused along with absconding accused Sameer on above mentioned date, time and place in furtherance of their common intention, used criminal force to daughter of complainant intending to outrage her modesty and thereby committed an offence punishable under Sec. 354, 354(A)(B)(D) r/w.34 of IPC? 3. Does the prosecution prove that the In the negative. accused along with absconding accused Sameer on above mentioned date, time and place committed sexual assault on complainant's daughter and thereby committed an offence punishable under Sec. 8,12 of The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act? 4. What Order ? As per final order. REASONS AS TO POINT NOS. 1 to 6 :­ 7. That, in order to establish the guilt of accused, prosecution has examined in all two witnesses. P.W.1 Manju Dayaram Garg, Complainant­ mother of victim girl is examined at Exh.11. P.W.2 Shraddha Ashok Waydande–A.P.I.is examined at Exh. 12­ Investigating officer. Prosecution has closed its evidence by filing pursis Exh.15. 5 Spl. Case(POCSO) No. 83/2016... Judgment CNR No. MHTH01­002238 ­2016 8. In support of the contention, prosecution has produced arrest­cum­personal search panchanama Exh.13, arrest panchanama Exh.14 9. P.W.1 complainant repeatedly deposed in her evidence before the court that she does not want to proceed with the matter. Hence, evidence of prosecution side is closed. P.W.1 deposed in her evidence that on 10.08.2015 at about 4.00 to 5.00 p.m., one missed call received on phone of her husband. Then one message was received at about 7.30 p.m. “ Payal Tu neeche aao, tuzse bat karni hai”. Accordingly, her daughter went on ground floor. Accused No.1 and absconding accused Sameer had taken her in auto rickshaw forcibly to Upvan. One accused removed her clothes. One accused caught hold her hand and pressed her mouth and moved hand on her person. Her daughter did not feel well. Accused kissed her daughter. Her daughter started shouting and told the accused to reach her to the house. Accordingly, accused had reached her to her house at about 10.00 p.m. Accused threatened her donot disclose this fact to your parents, otherwise they will kill her and her parents. Therefore, she did not disclose the incident to them. Thereafter accused had given missed call. On one occasion, complainant herself replied the missed call. Accused talked with her. At that time, complainant came to know that the accused persons are working near her house. She identified the accused present before the court. Then, she lodged report at Mahila Nari Shakti. After that she lodged report at police station on 19.08.2015. 6 Spl. Case(POCSO) No. 83/2016... Judgment CNR No. MHTH01­002238 ­2016 10. It is to be noted that the report was lodged against two accused. However, one accused is absconding. Therefore, charge­ sheet is filed against only one accused Sameer Pophalkar. 11. P.W.2 Investigating Officer deposed that she had investigated this matter. She had recorded statement of witness in question answer form. Then, she had recorded statement of other witnesses. Accused was arrested by her and prepared arrest panchanama. She identified the accused present before the court. 12. As per prosecution story that by giving missed call and by giving message to the victim accused had called the victim. However, in the report of complainant specific message is not mentioned. On the contrary, P.W.1 specifically stated in her examination­in­chief that accused had given message “Payal Tu Neeche Aao, tuze bat karni hai.” This contradiction is brought on record by the Ld. Advocate for accused in cross­examination of the complainant. There is nothing on record on the part of prosecution that call record of the mobile number of complainant's husband and accused have been collected and produced on record. Therefore, this fact is not proved by the prosecution. Incident took place on 10.08.2014. Report was lodged on 19.08.2014. She admitted in her cross­examination that after the incident on 13.08.2014, she had called the accused near her house. When she was asked whether 4 to 5 persons were went to beat the accused, she replied that accused did not come there. They all were searching the accused. Thereafter, one meeting was called in the office of Kishor 7 Spl. Case(POCSO) No. 83/2016... Judgment CNR No. MHTH01­002238 ­2016 Jadhav, Journalist during the period of 10.08.2014/2015 to 29.08.2014/2015. Accused did not attend the meeting. From this evidence it is clear that after the incident complainant tried to meet with the accused. However, as per her statement, he has not attended the meeting. 13. Evidence of P.W.1 is hearsay evidence. Prosecution has not examined victim. Her statement u/s.164 of Cr.P.C. is produced on record. Investigating Officer deposed that she has recorded her statement in question answer form. Complainant is not eye witness. As per narration of the victim she has lodged report and deposed before the court. However, victim is not examined before the court. In the cross­examination complainant admitted that her daughter is residing in Delhiand she has to close this matter. Except the evidence of complainant and investigating officer, prosecution has not examined any other witness. Victim is the star witness in this matter. In absence of oral as well as documentary evidence, it is difficult for me to hold that accused has committed offence. Hence, I come to the conclusion that the prosecution has failed to prove the guilt of accused. Hence, I answer point Nos.1 to 3 in the negative and proceed to pass the following order : ORDER 1. Accused Sameer Prakash Pophalkar is hereby acquitted under section 235 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, for the offences punishable under sections 363, 354, 354 (A)(B) (D) of Indian Penal Code, S. 8, 12 of Protection of Children from 8 Spl. Gaikwad for Accused ================================= :: J U D G M E N T ;; (Delivered on this 11th day of December, 2017) 1. Accused is facing charge for the offence punishable under Section 354, 342 and 452 of Indian Penal Code (hereinafter referred as IPC) and U/sec.7 & 8 of The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (hereinafter referred as POCSO Act). 2. Name of the victim, full name of her family members, place of incidence, name of school are not mentioned in the judgment to avoid disclosure of identity of Victim as per Section 33(7) of the POCSO Act. 3. The prosecution story in brief is as follows :­ 3.1. The informant Ramesh has lodged FIR on 10.3.15 with Rabale Police Station stating that he used to reside with his wife, Two son and One daughter. He further stated that victim aged about 15 years old is a daughter of his brother­in­law, used to reside with him. It is further stated that on 4.3.15 his wife alongwith younger son went to Gujarat for :3 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) Holi festival and therefore they used to keep elder son and daughter with Anandi Mavji Verat (wife of accused) who is his neighbor. 3.2. It is alleged that on 5.3.2015 accused Mavji came to his house at about 11 a.m. when the Victim was alone. He demanded water and she given it to him. When Victim went to kitchen to arrange utensils accused closed the main door of house and entered into kitchen and caught hold her hand and moved his hand on her breast and made sexual comment. That time she pushed him and went outside of the house immediately. 3.3. It is further alleged that at about 10 p.m when he returned to the house that victim narrated the incidence regarding sexual assault by accused. It is further alleged that he stated the said incidence to his partner Dhanji and Dhanji advised him to inform the incidence to father of victim. As per his advice he communicated all the incidence to father of victim. The father of victim told him that he is coming to Mumbai after Holi. Accordingly on 9.3.15 at about 4.30 p.m Father of victim came to the house of informant. Thereafter victim communicated all the incidence to her father and :4 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) thereafter he has lodged F.I.R against accused. 3.4. On the basis of said FIR C.R.No.I­ 83/15 came to be registered in Rabale Police Station for the offence punishable u/sec.354, 342 and 452 of Indian Penal Code and U/sec.7 & 8 of The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. 4. After completion of investigation, charge­sheet was filed against accused for the offence punishable u/sec.354, 342 and 452 of Indian Penal Code and U/sec.7 & 8 of The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. 5. The charge against accused was framed vide Ex.6 for the offences punishable u/sec.354, 342 and 452 of Indian Penal Code and U/sec.7 & 8 of The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 and explained the contents thereof to accused in vernacular. Accused pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. 6. The prosecution examined in all 5 witnesses to prove the guilt of accused for the above mentioned offences. The incriminating circumstances emerges from the prosecution evidence were put to accused in his examination U/sec.313 of Cr.P.C. He denied all the allegations. The defence of accused gathered from the cross­examination and statement u/sec.313 is that of total :5 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) denial and false implication to avoid repayment of the hand loan. 7. Heard learned APP Smt.Hivrale for prosecution and Adv. Shri.Gaikwad for defence. Considering the charge, evidence and argument following points arise for my determination and I recorded my findings with reasons as follows:­ S.No. Points Findings 1. Whether the prosecution proves Yes. that victim was a "child" as per Sec.2 (1) (d) of POCSO Act, on the date of incidence? 2. Whether the prosecution proves Yes. that on 5.3.15 at about 11 to 11.30a.m. accused used criminal force to victim intending to outrage her modesty and thereby committed offence punishable under 354 of I.P.C.? 3. Whether the prosecution proves Yes. that accused wrongfully confined victim minor girl and thereby committed offence punishable u/sec.342 of IPC. :6 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) 4. Whether the prosecution proves Yes. that accused committed house trespass by entering into the house of informant used as a human dwelling having made preparation for causing hurt to said minor victim and thereby committed an offence U/sec.452 of I.P.C 5. Whether the prosecution proves Yes. that accused committed sexual assault on the minor victim and thereby committed an offence u/sec.7 punishable with Sec. 8 of POCSO Act? 6. What order ? As per final order : R E A SO N S : 8. To establish guilt of accused prosecution has examined in all following 5 witnesses. P.W. Exh.No. Name of the witness PW.No.1 10 Ramesh ­ Informant. PW.No.2 13 The Victim PW.No.3 16 Mukesh Premji Patel­ panch witness. :7 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) PW.No.4 18 Santosh Narayan Pimple ­ Investigating Officer. PW.No.5 23 Mukesh Tukaram Pashte ­ In­ charge Principal of school. 9. The prosecution also relied on following documentary evidence:­ Sr.No. Particulars Exh.No 1 FIR 12 2 Spot panchanama 17 3 Admission form 24 4 Register of School 25 5 Birth Certificate Article 5A 6 School Leaving Certificate 26 AS TO POINT NO.1 10. Accused is charged for the offence punishable under provisions of POCSO Act along with I.P.C. For the application of POCSO Act the prosecution is bound to prove that the victim is child within the meaning of S.2 (1)(d) of POCSO Act. Further there is a statutory presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act, which requires the Court to presume that the offence was committed if the offences are alleged under Sections 3, 5, 7 and 9 of the POCSO Act. The Section reads as; "29. Presumption as to certain offences. ­ Where a :8 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) person is prosecuted for committing or abetting or attempting to commit any offence under sections 3,5,7 and section 9 of this Act, the Special Court shall presume, that such person has committed or abetted or attempted to commit the offence, as the case may be, unless the contrary is proved." 11. So in view of the special presumption in POCSO Act, before dealing with the other evidence and allegations, it is necessary to answer the point whether prosecution proved that the victim is/was minor at the time of incidence. 12. The learned SPP submitted that prosecution has proved that the victim is a child within the meaning of clause (1) (d) of Section 2 of POCSO Act by ocular evidence of PW­2 Victim and PW­5 Mr. Pashte along with documentary evidence Exh. 25 to 26 and Verified copy of Birth Certificate at Article No. 5A. She further submitted that the witness has brought original Birth Certificate alongwith him and get it verified from the officer of the court and placed on record. Birth Certificate being public document, to prove that no formal proof thereof is required. She relied on unreported judgment of honorable Bombay High court in Santosh Suresh Modi vs. State of Maharashtra,Criminal Appeal No. 414 of 2011 decided on 2nd March, 2017 wherein, in para 11 and 12 observed as follows :­ :9 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) "11 Perusal of the certificate at Exhibit 74 issued by Vita Municipal Council shows that prosecutrix was born to P.W.1­Ravindra Jagtap on 19.1.1993. This certificate was issued on 25.5.1995. Certificate at Exhibit 74 is issued by the Registrar acting under the provisions of Registration of Birth and Death Act, 1969. Section 7 of the said Act deals with appointment of Registrars for each local area comprising the area within the jurisdiction of a municipality, panchayat or other local authority. It is the duty of the Registrar to register every birth and every death which takes place in his jurisdiction. This act mandates that the Registrar should discharge his duties carefully. Section 8 of this Act mandates each head of the house to report birth in the family to the Registrar. This Act provides for his maintenance of register for recording birth and death within the local area. In pursuant to the provisions of Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, certificate at Exhibit 74 came to be issued by the Registrar as per provisions of Sections 12 as well as 17 of the said Act. The certificate at Exhibit 74 as such is issued by the Public Officer and it is a document forming the record of the acts of the Public Officer and therefore the same is a public document within the meaning of the said term as per provisions of Section 74 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. State of M.P., (2010) 8 SCC 191 honorable Supreme Court discussed about legal issue sole evidence of Victim in sexual offences as follows :­ “ Sole evidence of prosecutrix 9. In State of Maharashtra v. Chandraprakash Kewalchand Jain [(1990) 1 SCC 550 : 1990 SCC (Cri) 210 : AIR 1990 SC 658] this Court held that a woman, who is the victim of sexual assault, is not an accomplice to the crime but is a victim of another person's lust and, therefore, her evidence need not be tested with the same amount of suspicion as that of an accomplice. The Court observed as under: (SCC p. 559, para 16) : 21 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) “16. A prosecutrix of a sex offence cannot be put on par with an accomplice. She is in fact a victim of the crime. The Evidence Act nowhere says that her evidence cannot be accepted unless it is corroborated in material particulars. She is undoubtedly a competent witness under Section 118 and her evidence must receive the same weight as is attached to an injured in cases of physical violence. The same degree of care and caution must attach in the evaluation of her evidence as in the case of an injured complainant or witness and no more. What is necessary is that the court must be alive to and conscious of the fact that it is dealing with the evidence of a person who is interested in the outcome of the charge leveled by her. If the court keeps this in mind and feels satisfied that it can act on the evidence of the prosecutrix, there is no rule of law or practice incorporated in the Evidence Act similar to Illustration (b) to Section 114 which requires it to look for corroboration. If for some reason the court is hesitant to place implicit reliance on the testimony of the prosecutrix it may look for evidence which may lend assurance to her testimony short of corroboration required in the case of an accomplice. The nature of evidence required to lend assurance to the testimony of the prosecutrix must necessarily depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. But if a prosecutrix is an adult and of full understanding the court is entitled to base a conviction on her evidence unless the same is shown to be infirm and not trustworthy. If the totality of the circumstances appearing on the record of the case disclose that the prosecutrix does not have a strong motive to falsely involve the person charged, the court should ordinarily have no : 22 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) hesitation in accepting her evidence.” 10. In State of U.P. v. Pappu [(2005) 3 SCC 594 : 2005 SCC (Cri) 780] this Court held that even in a case where it is shown that the girl is a girl of easy virtue or a girl habituated to sexual intercourse, it may not be a ground to absolve the accused from the charge of rape. It has to be established that there was consent by her for that particular occasion. Absence of injury on the prosecutrix may not be a factor that leads the court to absolve the accused. This Court further held that there can be conviction on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix and in case, the court is not satisfied with the version of the prosecutrix, it can seek other evidence, direct or circumstantial, by which it may get assurance of her testimony. The Court held as under: (SCC p. 597, para 12) “12. It is well settled that a prosecutrix complaining of having been a victim of the offence of rape is not an accomplice after the crime. There is no rule of law that her testimony cannot be acted upon without corroboration in material particulars. She stands at a higher pedestal than an injured witness. In the latter case, there is injury on the physical form, while in the former it is both physical as well as psychological and emotional. However, if the court of facts finds it difficult to accept the version of the prosecutrix on its face value, it may search for evidence, direct or circumstantial, which would lend assurance to her testimony. Assurance, short of corroboration as understood in the context of an accomplice, would do.” 11. In State of Punjab v. Gurmit Singh [(1996) 2 SCC 384 : 1996 SCC (Cri) 316 : AIR 1996 SC 1393] this Court held that in cases involving : 23 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) sexual harassment, molestation, etc. the court is duty­bound to deal with such cases with utmost sensitivity. Minor contradictions or insignificant discrepancies in the statement of a prosecutrix should not be a ground for throwing out an otherwise reliable prosecution case. Evidence of the victim of sexual assault is enough for conviction and it does not require any corroboration unless there are compelling reasons for seeking corroboration. The court may look for some assurances of her statement to satisfy judicial conscience. The statement of the prosecutrix is more reliable than that of an injured witness as she is not an accomplice. The Court further held that the delay in filing FIR for sexual offence may not be even properly explained, but if found natural, the accused cannot be given any benefit thereof. The Court observed as under: (SCC pp. 394­96 & 403, paras 8 & 21) “8. … The court overlooked the situation in which a poor helpless minor girl had found herself in the company of three desperate young men who were threatening her and preventing her from raising any alarm. Again, if the investigating officer did not conduct the investigation properly or was negligent in not being able to trace out the driver or the car, how can that become a ground to discredit the testimony of the prosecutrix? The prosecutrix had no control over the investigating agency and the negligence of an investigating officer could not affect the credibility of the statement of the prosecutrix. … The courts must, while evaluating evidence, remain alive to the fact that in a case of rape, no self­respecting woman would come forward in a court just to make a humiliating statement against her honor such as : 24 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) is involved in the commission of rape on her. In cases involving sexual molestation, supposed considerations which have no material effect on the veracity of the prosecution case or even discrepancies in the statement of the prosecutrix should not, unless the discrepancies are such which are of fatal nature, be allowed to throw out an otherwise reliable prosecution case. … Seeking corroboration of her statement before relying upon the same, as a rule, in such cases amounts to adding insult to injury. … Corroboration as a condition for judicial reliance on the testimony of the prosecutrix is not a requirement of law but a guidance of prudence under given circumstances. … *** 21. … The courts should examine the broader probabilities of a case and not get swayed by minor contradictions or insignificant discrepancies in the statement of the prosecutrix, which are not of a fatal nature, to throw out an otherwise reliable prosecution case. If evidence of the prosecutrix inspires confidence, it must be relied upon without seeking corroboration of her statement in material particulars. If for some reason the court finds it difficult to place implicit reliance on her testimony, it may look for evidence which may lend assurance to her testimony, short of corroboration required in the case of an accomplice. The testimony of the prosecutrix must be appreciated in the background of the entire case and the trial court must be alive to its responsibility and be sensitive while dealing with cases involving sexual molestations.” 12. In State of Orissa v. Thakara Besra [(2002) 9 SCC 86 : 2003 SCC (Cri) 1080 : AIR 2002 SC : 25 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) 1963] this Court held that rape is not mere physical assault, rather it often distracts (sic destroys) the whole personality of the victim. The rapist degrades the very soul of the helpless female and, therefore, the testimony of the prosecutrix must be appreciated in the background of the entire case and in such cases, non­examination even of other witnesses may not be a serious infirmity in the prosecution case, particularly where the witnesses had not seen the commission of the offence. 13. In State of H.P. v. Raghubir Singh [(1993) 2 SCC 622 : 1993 SCC (Cri) 674] this Court held that there is no legal compulsion to look for any other evidence to corroborate the evidence of the prosecutrix before recording an order of conviction. Evidence has to be weighed and not counted. Conviction can be recorded on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix, if her evidence inspires confidence and there is absence of circumstances which militate against her veracity. A similar view has been reiterated by this Court in Wahid Khan v. State of M.P. [(2010) 2 SCC 9 : (2010) 1 SCC (Cri) 1208] placing reliance on an earlier judgment in Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan [AIR 1952 SC 54 : 1952 Cri LJ 547] . 14. Thus, the law that emerges on the issue is to the effect that the statement of the prosecutrix, if found to be worthy of credence and reliable, requires no corroboration. The court may convict the accused on the sole testimony of the prosecutrix.” 24. The said crime was handed over to him for investigation immediately. 32.2. At about 00.50 a.m he arrested accused. Thereafter he prepared spot panchanama Ex.17 on the spot in presence of panch witnesses, recorded statement of witnesses and also obtained copy of school leaving certificate of victim to show her age. After investigation he found sufficient evidence against accused therefore he filed chargesheet against accused. He identified the accused before the court. : 36 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) 32.3. In his cross examination he admitted that at the time of recording FIR informant has not given any documentary evidence regarding age of victim. She has stated specifically her age as 15 years old. Though she stated her birth date he did not written it in her statement. He denied the suggestion that on 10.3.15 at the time of lodging FIR victim and her father were present. He did not investigate whether there is any economic transactions between informant and accused. 33. It is further submitted on behalf of accused that though Victim was available on 10.3.15 her statement was not recorded immediately, but recorded on 14.3.15 which makes prosecution case doubtful. PW­2 Victim has deposed that she was in police station along with informant on 10.3.15. But PW­4 Investigating officer denied that she was in police station. From the evidence it is came on record that though she was available, Investigating officer has not recorded her statement on 10.3.15. If the investigating officer did not conduct the investigation properly or was negligent in immediate recording in statement, how can that become a ground to discredit the testimony of the Victim? The victim had no control over the investigating agency and the negligence : 37 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) of an investigating officer could not affect the credibility of the statement of the Victim. No self­respecting minor girl would come forward in a court just to make a humiliating statement against her honor for the benefit of other as suggested by the accused. No father would allow a minor girl to make such false allegations for the benefit of other. 34. In C. Muniappan v. State of Tamil Nadu, (2010) 9 SCC 567, this Court explained the law on this point in the following manner: “There may be highly defective investigation in a case. However, it is to be examined as to whether there is any lapse by the IO and whether due to such lapse any benefit should be given to the accused. The law on this issue is well settled that the defect in the investigation by itself cannot be a ground for acquittal. If primacy is given to such designed or negligent investigations or to the omissions or lapses by perfunctory investigation, the faith and confidence of the people in the criminal justice administration would be eroded. Where there has been negligence on the part of the investigating agency or omissions, etc. which resulted in defective investigation, there is a legal obligation on the part of the court to examine the prosecution evidence dehors such lapses, carefully, to find out whether the said evidence is reliable or not and to what extent it is reliable and as to whether such lapses affected the object of finding out the truth. Therefore, the investigation is not : 38 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) the solitary area for judicial scrutiny in a criminal trial. The conclusion of the trial in the case cannot be allowed to depend solely on the probity of investigation.” 35. It is suggested to PW­1 informant that prior to 5.3.15 he has received loan of Rs.1 lakh from Mavji and to avoid repayment he filed false case and PW­2 Victim is deposing false against accused at the instance of Informant. However, in statement under S. 313 of Cr.P.C. accused came with a case that on 5.3.15 at about 9.30 a.m. informant took hand loan of Rs. 1,00,000/­ on a promise of repayment within one or two days. But it is pertinent to note that at the time of cross­examination of PW­1 informant, accused has not given suggestion that on 5.3.15 at about 9.30 a.m. informant took hand loan. Further it is suggested to PW­4 Investigating officer that he did not investigate whether there is any economic transactions between informant and accused. But it is not the case of accused that he informed investigating officer regarding alleged hand loan economic transaction at the time of investigation. The extract of personal diary of accused is not believable. There is no acknowledgment of informant. Because it is very easy to prepare. The entries therein are without any details and appears to be in cash without any valid proof of there truthfulness. Accused has : 39 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) not brought his income tax return or balance­sheet showing liability of informant. 36. The accused himself brought in cross examination of PW­ 1 informant that before incidence he was having very good relations with accused. It is come on record on the day of incidence also the minor children of informant were with the wife of accused. So considering close family relations there was no reason for false implication of accused by informant. 37. As already discussed, delay in the lodging of the FIR has been satisfactorily explained and found acceptable by this Court. The evidence of the victim being consistent thereby inspires confidence and needs no further corroboration. Nevertheless, by way of abundant caution, the evidence of the other prosecution witnesses have also been considered. 38. Above all, this Court finds reasons to raise a presumption that the accused had committed the crime, as provided in Section 29 of the POCSO Act. Of course, the said presumption is rebuttable. But, in this case, the accused has not rebutted the said presumption either by means of direct evidence or by means of circumstantial evidence. Thus, by means of the said unrebutted presumption also, : 40 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) the prosecution has proved beyond reasonable doubt that accused has committed the offence. 39. From the evidence on record, I come to the conclusion that, prosecution has proved offence U/sec.354, 342 and 452 of Indian Penal Code and U/sec.7 & 8 of The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 beyond reasonable doubt. Hence, I answer Point No.2 to 5 in affirmative. 40. As I hold that prosecution proved the guilt of accused for the offence punishable u/sec.354, 342 and 452 of Indian Penal Code and U/sec.7 & 8 of The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, beyond reasonable doubt, I stop here to hear the accused on the point of sentence. Thane ( Prakash R. Kadam ) Dated: 11.12.2017 Designated Judge Under Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 for Thane 41. Heard accused and his Advocate Shri.B. W. Gaikwad on the point of sentence. Accused submitted that there is no criminal background. He is only earning member of his family consisting wife, two minor children and brother : 41 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) and his entire family is also dependent upon him. Hence, he prayed for leniency. 42. Ld. Spl. Public Prosecutor submitted that, offence is of serious nature. She prayed for maximum punishment prescribed by law. 43. So considering facts and circumstances of the present case I find that, a facts in case in hand do not warrant maximum punishment prescribed under law. Hence, I am of the view that following punishment would meet the ends of justice. Hence I proceed to pass following order :­ :: ORDER :: 1. Accused Mavji Lalji Verat is hereby convicted u/sec.235(2) of Cr.P.C. for the offence punishable under Sec. 354 of Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer 2 years Rigorous Imprisonment and fine of Rs.5000/­. In default of fine to suffer Simple imprisonment for 15 days. : 42 : SPL.C. No.60/2015 (Judgement) 3. 1 Cri.Bail Apln.No. 814/2016 (order below Exhibit 1) Criminal Bail Application No.814/2016 Ramaasare Chouhan .. Applicant versus The State of Maharashtra (Through Kalwa Police Station) .. Non­applicant ORDER BELOW EXHIBIT 1 1] By this application the applicant is seeking regular bail under section 439 of Cr.P.C. who was arrested on 05/03/2016 by Kalwa Police Station in connection with C.R.No.I­76/2016 registered for an offence punishable under section 376 of I.P.C. and section 4,8,9(m) of The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (hereinafter in short referred to as P.O.C.S.O. Act). 2] Heard learned Advocate Mr. Iqbal Abdulla for the applicant/accused and Spl.PP Mrs.S.E.Phad. I.O. present with case diary. 3] The F.I.R. came to be registered on 04/03/2016 at the instance of the informant/mother of the victim­girl aged about 5 years with an indictment that on 01/03/2016 accused was inappropriately touching private part of her minor daughter and behaving inappropriately with her by undressing her. 2 Cri.Bail Apln.No. 814/2016 (order below Exhibit 1) 4] The learned Counsel for the applicant submitted that the applicant/accused is falsely implicated. He submitted that there is delay of 4 days in lodging F.I.R. The incident is stated to be dated 01/03/2016 and F.I.R. is lodged on 04/03/2016 without any explanation. He further submitted that complaint is after thought. In fact, on 03/03/2016 the informant lodged complaint against the accused which was registered as Non cognizable offence wherein no such allegations are made. He further submitted that there is no medical evidence. The accused is in jail since 40 days. The investigation is almost completed. The accused is permanent resident of Thane and he is ready to abide any conditions imposed by the Court and prayed for releasing him on bail. 5] Per contra, the ld. Spl.P.P. opposed the application submitting that the offence is serious in respect of minor girl aged about 5 years. She further submitted that the accused is aged about 55 years and committed rape on a minor girl of 5 years. The medical certificate clearly shows that the minor girl has been subjected to sexual assault. The investigation is still in progress. The offence is serious and there are chances of tampering of witnesses and hampering of investigation and prayed for rejected of the application. 6] Upon hearing and perusal of F.I.R., it appears that initially, the F.I.R. was registered with an indictment that accused was witnesses by the informant behaving most 3 Cri.Bail Apln.No. 814/2016 (order below Exhibit 1) inappropriately with her minor daughter by touching her private part and by making her undressed. It appears that the accused is of the advanced aged man of 55 years and a neighbour of informant and by taking victim­girl to his house, he committed the alleged act with the tendered aged girl of 5 years. The medical certificate of the victim­girl clearly shows that she was subject to sexual assault and medical officer had given clear opinion about signs of confirmed vaginal penetration. The hymen of the victim­girl appears to be ruptured and torn. The delay in lodging of F.I.R. as well as lodging of any N.C. against the accused, cannot be considered at this stage as the investigation is in progress. Moreover, the informant herself witnesses the incident and at the time of incident two other children were also present in the house of accused. Accused and tender aged victim­girl are neighbourers. Thus, there is strong prima­facie case against the accused and the investigation is at nascent stage. As there are serious allegations against the accused, the apprehension of learned A.P.P. about tampering of witnesses and hampering of investigation is well founded. Hence, absolutely no case is made out to release the accused on bail. Hence, I pass following order:­ ORDER The application stands rejected. Thane. Date : 19/04/2016. (Ms. U.M. Nandeshwar) Special Judge (P.O.C.S.O. Act), Thane.

.. 1 .. bail 804/2015 (Order below Exhibit 1) Order below Exh.1 in Criminal Bail Application No. 804/2015 This application is filed by applicant namely Zubiar s/o Kasam Khan for his release on bail under section 439 of Cr.P.C. in connection with C.R.No.I­123/2015 registered at Vashi police station on the basis of the complaint for offence punishable under section 354A of I.P.C. and section 8 of Protection of Children From Sexual Offence Act, 2012 (hereinafter in short P.O.C.S.O. Act). It was contended and argued that the applicant is arrested in connection with this crime on the complaint filed with the allegation that the applicant was indulged in activity of molestation of minor victim girls. It is further contended and argued that the applicant is falsely implicated in this crime. It is further submitted that the applicant is permanent resident of the address given and that if the present applicant/accused is released on bail, he will co­ operate with the investigation and will not tamper with prosecution evidence and will not abscond and therefore the applicant is entitled to be released on bail. 2] The application is objected to on behalf of prosecution by filing reply and it was contended and argued that the accused used to follow the victim girl and her friends while they were going to school. It is also contended and argued that he was stalking the victim and her friends by pretending that he was talking on mobile while standing in the crowd. It is further contended and argued that the accused had molested the victim girls by inserting hand in the skirt and touching private part. It is further submitted that in such circumstance if the applicant/accused is released on bail, there is possibility of the applicant threatening the complainant and .. 2 .. bail 804/2015 (Order below Exhibit 1) victim and other prosecution witnesses. It is also contended that if the applicant is released on bail he may abscond and will not be available for trial. It was therefore contended that the applicant is not entitled to be released on bail. 3] As is clear, though the offences charged against the applicant/accused is of serious nature under section 354D of I.P.C. and section 8 of P.O.C.S.O. Act with the allegation that he had molested 10 years old girl, the fact cannot be overlooked that in the complaint it is mentioned that the girl stated to her mother that the person committing such act was unknown person and then it is alleged that next time they kept watch and caught the accused and in the light of that the submissions on behalf of applicant/accused that he was caught by the complainant only on the say of the girl since he was looking identical to the said unknown person and it is case of misidentification and that he is falsely implicated in this crime etc. are required to be considered on merits on the basis of evidence after trial. Even nothing is stated to be recovered from the applicant/accused. 4] Then, it is also well settled that at this stage of deciding bail application the evidence on record need not be scrutinized in detail and the main criteria to be considered is whether the applicant would be available for trial and whether there is any possibility of the applicant tampering with prosecution evidence if he is released on bail. 5] In that respect it is contended by the applicant that he is permanent resident of the address given and he will not abscond .. 3 .. bail 804/2015 (Order below Exhibit 1) if released on bail and that he is ready to abide by any conditions imposed. 6] Then, though it is submitted on behalf of the prosecution that the offence is of serious nature and the possibility of the applicant/accused being absconded or tampering with prosecution evidence is there, that aspect can be taken care of by saddling certain conditions and on that ground the application cannot be rejected. 7] Then, it has also to be mentioned that the investigation in the matter though almost completed, the charge sheet is yet to be submitted and it would take time to complete the investigation and submit the charge sheet and then to conclude the trial in the matter and looking to the fact that the matter is comparatively new one, it would take longer time to dispose of the matter and there is no point in keeping the applicants/accused in jail for uncertain period. 8] In all such circumstance I am of the view that this is a fit case wherein the applicant can be released on bail. JUDGMENT (Delivered on 16th day of February, 2018.) 1] Accused stands prosecuted by police station officer A.P.M.C., Navi Mumbai for the charge of offences for kidnapping, outraging modesty and penetrative sexual assault punishable u/sec. 363,354(A) of Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.) and U/s. 7 punishable U/s. 8 ..2/- ..2.. Before 15 days of the incident victim went to the house of her maternal uncle namely; Kisan Jorsingh Bhide at Turbhe, Navi Mumbai for attending some program in his house. They took search of victim in the nearby area. Also they enquired with their relatives on phone but they could not find victim. On that day Kisan Bhide received phone call of uncle of accused and enquired about victim and told him that accused is also not at home. On that, he tried to contact with the accused on his mobile but his mobile was switched off. Thereafter, he confirmed that accused has kidnapped his daughter. Therefore, he lodged report in A.P.M.C. police station. On the basis of complaint of Shri Mofatlal Amrut Dange, Crime No.I­ 39/2017 punishable U/secs. 363 of I.P.C came to be registered. 3] On 05/02/2017 Lady PSI Dhanashree Pawar enquired with victim and recorded her statement in presence of Member, Mahila Dakshata Samiti, Turbhe, Navi Mumbai and her mother. In her statement before police and in presence of Medical Officer of Municipal Corporation Hospital, Vashi victim stated that accused outraged her modesty and committed sexual assault on her at Lonavala in one Lodge. ..3/- ..3.. SPL.C.No.90/2017 (Exh.No.19) CNR No. MHTH01­002254­2017 Therefore, section­ 354(A)of I.P.Code and sections 8 & 12 of POCSO Act were added. Investigation was carried out by API Shri. D.D. Chaskar Thereafter he prepared spot panchanama, recorded statements of witnesses and collected bonafide certificate of victim from Z.P. School, Ambedkarnagar, sent muddemal to F.S.L. for chemical analysis. After completion of investigation he submitted the charge­sheet before Sessions Court, Thane. 4] Charge Exh.9 was framed and explained to the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried. His defence is that of total denial. 5] Considering the case of the prosecution following points arise for my determination and I have recorded my findings thereon for the reasons discussed below. POINTS FINDINGS 1 Does the prosecution prove that on 03/02/2017 at about 15.30 hours at room No.2 first floor, Devkikumbh apartment, Plot No. 518, sector­22, turbhe, Navi No. Mumbai, accused kidnapped victim from the lawful guardianship of her parents and thereby committed an offence punishable u/sec. 363of I.P.C. ? 2 Does the prosecution further prove that on the above mentioned date, time and No. place accused used criminal force to victim with intent to outrage her modesty and thereby committed an offence punishable u/sec. 354­A of I.P.C. ? 3 Does the prosecution further prove that on the above mentioned date, time and No. ..4/- ..4.. SPL.C.No.90/2017 (Exh.No.19) CNR No. MHTH01­002254­2017 place accused committed sexual assault and sexual harassment on victim u/s.7 punishable U/s. 8 and U/s.11 punishable U/s. 12 of POCSO Act? 4 What order ? As per final order. REASONS Points Nos. 1 to 3 : 6] These points are inter­linked to each other hence, in order to avoid repetition of evidence, they are clubbed together. 7] Heard both the Ld. Counsels. Perused case record. Victim deposed at Exh.13 that as accused is residing in front of her house, she is knowing him. On seeing her, he used to make signal to her and used to tease her. The parents of accused came to her mother for proposal of his marriage with her. They refused the said proposal. Thereafter, accused used to give threats to her if she would not marry with him, he will kill her brother. 8] Victim further deposed that she went to her maternal uncle's house at Turbhe for marriage of his daughter. Accused came there for work to her maternal uncle. On the call of accused she came near the shop on the ground floor of the building where her maternal uncle resides and met accused at about 4.00 p.m. and thereafter, accused took her in rickshaw to Lonavala. 9] Considering the above evidence, I find no element of kidnapping by accused to victim as she on her own accord visited to ..5/- ..5.. SPL.C.No.90/2017 (Exh.No.19) CNR No. MHTH01­002254­2017 accused and then proceed to Lonavala. Therefore, the charge of offence U/s. 363 of I.P. Code is not proved by the prosecution. 10] Victim further deposed that accused took her to a Lodge in Lonavala and there he tried to outrage her modesty by moving his hand on her stomach, chest and kissed her. The cardinal principle of appreciation of evidence is that the evidence of the victim is to be considered whole as what stated by victim in her examination­in­chief is remained in force during her cross­examination. Therefore, I am inclined to advent on her cross­examination. In her cross­examination she deposed a different story that on 03/02/2017 she went alongwith her friend without informing her maternal uncle and after outing came back to the house on next day. She admitted that on 03/02/2017 accused did not kidnap her and he has not tried to outrage her modesty by moving his hand over her stomach and also not kissed her. Thus, the testimony of victim is not reliable and as such the charge for offence U/s. 354­A of I.P. Code is not proved by the prosecution. 11] Victim further deposed that she told her parents and brother about the incident and then her father lodged report. However, the father of victim (P.W.2) deposed that as victim was not traced out therefore, he lodged complaint. He is reluctant to the contents mentioned in the FIR and as such Ld. A.P.P. cross­examined him. In the cross­examination he admitted that out of Court there is settlement between him and accused. 12] The contention of victim is that as accused is residing in front of her house and his parents gave proposal of his marriage with ..6/- ..6..
